abstract: Population abundance is a central parameter in conservation, for which biased estimates can seriously undermine management strategies for threatened species. The tamaraw (Bubalus mindorensis) is a Critically Endangered large herbivore endemic to Mindoro Island, Philippines. The species has been monitored annually at Mounts Iglit-Baco Natural Park (MIBNP) since 2000 using a multi-vantage-point count method that is prone to both imperfect detection and repeated counting of the same individuals across sessions. Because the historical abundance estimation is an index of relative abundance with no probabilistic modeling of counts, the actual number of tamaraw in what is considered as the largest remaining population is still poorly known. To fill this gap, we conducted an independent double-observer experiment over five years (2022-2026) and fitted Bayesian hierarchical detection models to the counts. As expected, detection probability was <1 throughout (single-observer estimates 0.41-0.84; combined-observer 0.68-0.96), confirming that a substantial fraction of animals is missed by rangers during all counts. Compared with these estimates, historical counts overestimated tamaraw abundance by a factor of 1.61-2.34, yielding a mean population size across 2022-2026 of 203 individuals (95% credible interval 182-226) rather than the roughly 400-500 individuals previously assumed. Our results imply that the MIBNP tamaraw population, while more vulnerable to demographic and genetic risks than previously believed, has likely responded positively to ongoing conservation efforts; we recommend that population viability assessments and translocation plans for the species be revised accordingly.
